prize_parts.citation: For a visionary prose oeuvre in which memory, the body and dream are built into a large metaphysical architecture, from Blinding to Solenoid.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged, but it is more conditional than in round 1. The test I apply is whether a voice is audible in the writing and nowhere else, and whether the formal ambition and the imaginative depth are the same thing. On public knowledge and the longlist description, Blinding and Solenoid pass that test better than the other shortlisted entries. Memory, the body and dream are the structural principle of very large books, not their subject matter. The late novels seem to extend an earlier project, and this bears on sustained quality across an oeuvre. Attribution is clean, with one writer and Romanian as the writing language. After the exchange I would narrow the citation to the prose project and not claim the poetry. Several supporters, myself included, have said that our coverage of the poetry and early fiction is partial. A citation should claim only what the committee can defend, and the poetry can be mentioned as formative ground in the discussion without being credited. I have read the chair's questions as a request to test conditions, not to repeat preferences. My answer to the first is that the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid must each earn their length through structure and recurring imagery, and I think they do, but I cannot verify this. I have not independently verified any source.
statement.case_against: The reservations stand. Density, rhythm and long recursive syntax are exactly what translation is most likely to alter, so my sense of the voice is a sense of the translated voice. That is a real weakness when the criterion I care most about is hearing the voice. I cannot rule out that scale sometimes substitutes for structure in the longest books. The case for the whole oeuvre rests mostly on the late novels, so it is thinner than a claim of sustained quality across decades would require. Olsson's Adonis case is the clearest formal and linguistic transformation of a literary language on the list, and Sward's Carson case is the one the committee can test most directly in the original text. If credible evidence showed that the late Cărtărescu volumes repeat a method or that the architecture does not hold, I would move to Carson. I would not move to Adonis unless readers of Arabic could vouch for the later poetry.

responses.point: Olsson accepts the warning that influence does not prove merit, and says his case rests on what the work does with the Arabic poetic language. He argues that the translation problem applies to every leading candidate, so it should not count more heavily against Adonis than against others. He asks the committee to test whether the late Cărtărescu novels are consolidation or accumulation.
responses.response: I accept the correction on translation. My round-1 hesitation about ranking Adonis first on translated selections applies, in a different form, to Cărtărescu's prose, and I should not have implied that prose is safer. I would not count translation uncertainty more heavily against Adonis. I do keep a narrower evidentiary point: I can name specific structural features of the prose that I think survive translation, and I cannot do the same for Arabic prosody. That is a statement about my own limits, not a ranking of the achievements. Your consolidation-versus-accumulation question is the right test for my own choice, and I cannot answer it from the evidence supplied. I agree with you on citation scope. Wording for Adonis would need to stay on the poetry. If readers of Arabic could speak to the later collections, I would reconsider his position in my ordering, and he remains my second alternative.

responses.point: Sward argues that the continuity of concerns (grief, desire, the fragment and the afterlife of ancient texts) across essays, verse novel, elegy and later hybrid work is development and not repetition. She would keep the citation on Carson's own writing and treat the translations as evidence of voice. She also notes that Carson's English text is directly legible to the committee.
responses.response: That is the strongest answer to my round-1 question, and it moves Carson closer to Cărtărescu in my own weighing. The direct legibility of the English is a real advantage under the common-criteria standard, because the committee can test the voice without an intermediary. I still hold back on one point. Continuity of concern is not quite the same as sustained depth, and I cannot tell from the supplied evidence whether the smaller and occasional books reach the level of the signal books. I also think the citation problem remains, because the most inventive objects partly live in their design. For those reasons I keep Carson as my first alternative and not my first choice. I would change that if the committee could show that the lyric and essayistic work, read as text, carries the claim without the book-objects.

responses.point: Palm separates two risks. Uneven quality in some volumes is a question about sustained quality that can be tested against the major works. Translation loss is a question about whether the achievement can be seen at all. She asks that the committee say openly that its judgment is made through translation.
responses.response: I accept the distinction and the request for candour. Unevenness in minor volumes would not defeat the case if the Blinding trilogy and Solenoid carry it, and I think that is the right way to frame the claim. This also supports a prose-only citation, since the claim then rests on the volumes we can discuss best. The translation point I take more seriously than you suggest. If the voice cannot be seen at all, my main criterion cannot be applied, so the committee should state that its judgment is mediated and should welcome any readings from Romanian-language readers. I do not think that should count against Cărtărescu more than against the other two leading candidates.

responses.point: Carlberg holds that a prose project built on large-scale structure and recurring images is somewhat less exposed to translation loss than verse resting on prosody, and says this is a judgment she has not verified. She also asks whether the Adonis case should receive more weight than a translation-based reading allows.
responses.response: I share the unverified judgment, but after Olsson's reply I do not want to rest anything on it. We should apply one standard to B042, B017 and B007: translation uncertainty is real for each, and none of us can claim an advantage from it. On that common standard, what separates the candidates for me is the evidence about evenness and the scope of a defensible citation, not the translation problem. Your question about Adonis is a fair one for the committee, and I would answer it by seeking readers of the Arabic and not by guessing.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's voice, syntax and rhythm survives in the translations available to me, and whether the Romanian original would change my judgment.
Whether the very long late novels are evenly sustained or whether scale sometimes replaces structure. I cannot settle this from the supplied evidence.
How the poetry and early fiction compare with the later novels. My coverage is partial, which is why I narrowed the citation to the prose.
Whether the later poetry of Adonis holds the level of his major collections, and whether readers of Arabic would change the comparison.
How much of Carson's achievement is carried by her text and how much by book-object form, and whether a citation can be limited to her own writing.
Whether the committee could obtain readings in Romanian or Arabic. I do not assume such reports exist and have not seen any.
I rely on public knowledge and the longlist descriptions and have not independently verified any source or read the works for this exercise.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict requiring recusal is apparent from the supplied profile, and none is adjudicated here. The profile records no personal, professional or archival tie to any shortlisted writer. Her service with Sward since 2021, her work as a critic and novelist of historical fiction, and her stated regret at not being able to read some candidates in the original are context only. They are not evidence of a preference for any candidate. I note that Olsson and Sem-Sandberg have each disclosed scholarly or thematic interests that touch particular entries, and I do not treat those as conflicts either.
